seo_title: What Does an Insurance Umpire Do? Role, Process & Award
meta_description: What does an insurance umpire do? How umpires are chosen, how they resolve disputed items, and what their award means in Texas.
h1: What Does an Insurance Umpire Do in the Appraisal Process?
secondary_keywords: what does an insurance umpire do
excerpt: An insurance umpire is the neutral third member of an appraisal panel who decides items the two appraisers cannot agree on. Learn how umpires are chosen, how they work, and what their award means.
key_takeaways: An insurance umpire is a neutral third party who resolves disagreements between two appraisers.
The umpire usually decides only the items the appraisers cannot settle.
An award signed by the umpire and one appraiser generally sets the amount of loss.
Umpires decide amount of loss, not coverage, under Texas law.
body_html:
An insurance umpire is a neutral third party in the appraisal process who resolves disagreements between the policyholder's appraiser and the insurer's appraiser. The umpire reviews both estimates and the evidence, decides the disputed items, and signs an award. An award signed by the umpire and either appraiser generally sets the amount of loss.

What is the role of an insurance umpire?

Appraisal panels have three members. The policyholder chooses one appraiser, the insurance company chooses another, and those two appraisers select an umpire. Each appraiser works to establish an accurate amount of loss from their side's perspective. The umpire's job is to be the neutral decision-maker when they cannot agree.

Think of the insurance umpire as a tiebreaker with expertise. The umpire does not represent either side, does not advocate, and does not have a stake in the final number. Their only job is to decide fairly what the evidence supports.

In practice, the umpire does not usually build a third estimate from scratch. Instead, the two appraisers resolve as many items as they can on their own and send the remaining disputes to the umpire. The umpire then decides each disputed item based on the evidence.

The umpire's core responsibilities include:

  • Remaining impartial and independent from both parties
  • Reviewing the appraisers' estimates, photos, reports, and supporting documents
  • Inspecting the property when needed to see the damage firsthand
  • Asking questions and hearing each appraiser's explanation of disputed items
  • Deciding each unresolved item and signing a written award

Insurance umpire vs. appraiser: what is the difference?

Appraisers and umpires serve different roles on the same panel. The table below summarizes the main differences:

FactorAppraiserUmpire
Chosen byOne party (policyholder or insurer)The two appraisers, or a court
RoleDevelops and supports an estimate of lossNeutral decision-maker on disputes
When involvedFrom the start of appraisalUsually only when appraisers disagree
FeesPaid by the party who hired themUsually split equally between the parties
Signs awardYes, if they agree with itYes, when deciding disputed items

Neither role is the same as an insurance adjuster, who works for the carrier on the claim itself. For more on that distinction, read insurance appraiser vs. adjuster.

How is an insurance umpire chosen?

Most Texas policies require the two appraisers to agree on an umpire within a set time, often 15 days after both appraisers are named. Appraisers often exchange short lists of candidates and agree on someone both trust to be fair and knowledgeable.

If they cannot agree, either party can typically ask a court in the county where the property is located to appoint an umpire. Court appointment adds time and cost, so most appraisers work hard to agree.

Both sides should be comfortable with the choice. An umpire with a close business relationship to either party, or a history of working almost exclusively for carriers or for policyholders, may face objections. Ask your appraiser how the umpire was selected and whether any potential conflicts were disclosed.

A good umpire usually has deep experience with construction costs, estimating software, building codes, and the types of losses involved, whether hail, wind, water, or fire. See our full guide on how insurance umpires are chosen in Texas.

What happens when the umpire gets involved?

The umpire typically steps in after the appraisers have inspected the property and compared estimates. A common sequence looks like this:

  1. Submission. The appraisers send the umpire a list of agreed items and disputed items, along with their estimates and supporting evidence.
  2. Review. The umpire studies the documents, photos, measurement reports, engineering reports, and any code references.
  3. Inspection. The umpire may inspect the property, often with both appraisers present, to see contested damage.
  4. Presentations. Each appraiser explains its position on disputed items and answers questions.
  5. Decision. The umpire decides each disputed item and prepares or signs a written award.

Umpires generally decide items within the range the appraisers presented, but they are not required to simply split the difference. The better-supported position on each item usually carries more weight.

Tip: The umpire only knows what the appraisers show them. That is why your appraiser's documentation, photos, measurements, and line-item support matter so much when a dispute reaches the umpire.

What can an insurance umpire decide, and what can't they?

An umpire's authority is limited to what the appraisal clause allows. In Texas, State Farm Lloyds v. Johnson (Tex. 2009) established that appraisers and umpires decide the amount of loss. They may consider the extent of damage and whether damage was caused by the covered event, but they do not decide coverage or the insurer's liability.

Umpires commonly decide issues such as:

  • Whether a roof needs full replacement or can be repaired
  • Correct quantities, measurements, and waste factors
  • Pricing for materials and labor
  • Whether specific items, such as flashing or gutters, were damaged by the storm
  • Depreciation amounts and actual cash value

Umpires generally do not decide whether an exclusion applies, whether the policy was in force, or whether the insurer acted in bad faith. Those questions are handled outside appraisal. This is general information, not legal advice.

What does the umpire's award mean?

An appraisal award is a written statement of the amount of loss. When two of the three panel members sign it, it is generally binding on both parties as to amount. If the two appraisers agree on everything, the umpire may not sign at all. If they disagree, the award is typically signed by the umpire and one appraiser.

Awards often break out replacement cost, depreciation, and actual cash value, and may separate dwelling, other structures, and contents. Texas courts give awards strong deference and set them aside only in narrow circumstances, such as fraud, accident, or mistake. Learn more in is insurance appraisal legally binding in Texas.

Which disputes most often go to an insurance umpire?

Most appraisals involve a long list of items both sides accept quickly, plus a short list of high-dollar disagreements. On Texas property claims, the issues that most often reach the umpire include:

Roof replacement vs. repair

The carrier's appraiser may argue that a handful of shingles can be replaced, while the policyholder's appraiser shows that the roof cannot be repaired without causing more damage, or that the product is discontinued and cannot be matched. The umpire weighs photos, test square results, brittleness testing, and manufacturer information.

Hail damage vs. wear and tear

Because appraisers and umpires may address causation, a common dispute is whether marks on shingles, metal, or siding were caused by the storm or by age and foot traffic. Close-up photos, collateral damage on soft metals, and storm data help the umpire decide.

Interior damage and timing

If ceiling stains appeared weeks after the storm, the parties may disagree about whether they were caused by the covered event. A clear timeline and documentation of when stains were first noticed are essential.

Pricing and overhead

Disputes over unit prices, steep and high-roof labor, general contractor overhead and profit, and code-required items often come down to which side has better support. Local supplier quotes, building department letters, and comparable invoices give the umpire something concrete to rely on.

Whatever the issue, the insurance umpire is deciding between two positions, so each position needs its own evidence. An appraiser who simply says "this is too low" is at a disadvantage against one who shows exactly why.

Insurance umpires in Texas claims

Texas sees a high volume of appraisals because of frequent hail in Dallas-Fort Worth, Central Texas, and the Panhandle, plus hurricane and wind claims on the Gulf Coast. Umpires who handle Texas claims need to understand regional pricing, local building codes, and how materials like laminated shingles, metal roofing, and tile perform in Texas weather.

Texas law also affects what happens after the award. Under the Prompt Payment of Claims Act in Texas Insurance Code Chapter 542, insurers face deadlines for paying accepted claims. The Texas Supreme Court has held that paying an appraisal award does not automatically bar a prompt-payment claim (Barbara Technologies, 2019), though it generally bars most other extra-contractual claims (Ortiz, 2019).

When appraisers reach a deadlock, the umpire is what keeps the process moving. Read what happens if appraisers disagree and what an impasse in insurance appraisal is for more on how those situations unfold.

How much does an umpire cost?

Under most Texas policies, the policyholder and insurer split the umpire's fees equally, while each pays its own appraiser. Umpire fees vary with the size and complexity of the claim and may be charged hourly or as a flat or percentage-based fee.

Spending more on a well-prepared appraiser often reduces umpire costs. When the appraisers narrow the dispute to a short list of clearly defined items, the umpire spends less time reviewing and the process finishes sooner.

Because the umpire usually handles only the disputed items, a well-organized appraisal with fewer open issues can keep umpire costs down. Use our appraisal cost calculator to estimate whether appraisal makes financial sense for your claim.

Next steps: preparing for the umpire stage

If your claim is heading to appraisal, the strength of your appraiser's work will shape what the umpire sees. Clear photos, accurate measurements, code references, and a well-organized line-item estimate give the umpire solid ground to decide in your favor on disputed items.

faqs.q: Is an insurance umpire required in every appraisal?
faqs.a: No. If the two appraisers agree on the full amount of loss, they can sign the award themselves and the umpire never makes a decision. Many policies still require the appraisers to name an umpire early so one is ready if disputes arise. The umpire becomes active only when items remain unresolved.

faqs.q: Can the umpire side with my insurance company?
faqs.a: Yes. The umpire is neutral and decides each disputed item based on the evidence, so some items may go the insurer's way and others the policyholder's way. That is why a well-documented, line-item estimate from your appraiser is so important. The best-supported position on each item usually prevails.

faqs.q: Who can serve as an insurance umpire in Texas?
faqs.a: Umpires are typically experienced professionals such as former adjusters, appraisers, contractors, engineers, or attorneys with deep knowledge of construction costs and claims. They must be impartial and should not have a financial interest in the outcome. Policies may set additional qualifications, and courts can appoint an umpire when the appraisers cannot agree.

faqs.q: Can I talk directly to the umpire?
faqs.a: Generally, communication with the umpire flows through the appraisers, and both appraisers should be included in substantive discussions. Contacting the umpire privately can raise fairness concerns and may jeopardize the award. If you have information for the umpire, give it to your appraiser to present as part of the process.

faqs.q: How long does it take an umpire to decide?
faqs.a: It depends on the number of disputed items, the size of the loss, and scheduling. Many residential umpire decisions are made within a few weeks of receiving the appraisers' submissions and completing any inspection. Larger commercial losses with many disputed items can take longer, especially when multiple inspections are needed.
